To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the successful use of IAMs in the LRTAP convention depended on the institutional framework, which allowed for the development of the model, the recognition of its limits by all actors involved, and the ability to handle the uncertainties in the model and in policy.

(1) the RAINS model is a successful case of computer modelling in international policy; (2) the institutional framework built around the LRTAP convention and the EU facilitated this; (3) RAINS is a successful case because it was used as a policy tool in the negotiation process; and (4) the RAINS experience shows that computer models have their limits.

the use of computer-based Integrated Assessment Models in international environmental agreements can only be successful in cases where the institutional framework is well established, the models are well developed and the users of the models have a high level of self-awareness about their limitations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of IAMs in international environmental negotiations and the conditions for their success, with a particular focus on the LRTAP case.
the role and limits of computer modelling in the formulation and adoption of international environmental agreements.
how science and policy can be combined in the formulation of environmental policies, and how the use of computer modelling in this process is affected by the institutional setting.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of IAMs for IEAs is a very complex and difficult process, which is not fully understood, and for which there is no simple and straightforward recipe.

computer models are not the solution to environmental problems, but that they can be used in a limited way in a specific institutional context, and that the use of models should be accompanied by a thorough analysis of the uncertainties, distribution and ethical aspects of the issues.
the use of models in international policy-making is not a straightforward process.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the precautionary principle can be used as a political instrument, but it cannot substitute for the scientific analysis of uncertainty.
the use of computer modelling in international environmental policy is a complex process, and that its success depends on several conditions that need to be met.
the RAINS case shows that the use of IAMs in IEAs may be a success, but only if the model is well understood and its limits are fully appreciated.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the adoption of the precautionay principle in international environmental agreements should be based on a careful analysis of its implications, in particular on the distribution of costs and benefits among the parties involved.

the precautionary principle can be used in a positive manner, to help to define a common ground for negotiations and to avoid the use of the principle as an instrument to block international negotiations.
IAMs can be used in international negotiations to help to identify the most cost-effective policies.
